text: Where should error handling live in an agent workflow so that a failure is never silent? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the tool-call boundary, so a failing tool invocation is caught rather than ignored
options.why: Yes. The first boundary is where the agent calls out to a tool; an unhandled failure there propagates as confusing downstream behavior.

options.text: At the step and job level in the wrapping workflow, using explicit failure conditions instead of letting execution continue
options.why: Yes. Failing fast at the step level prevents partial or inconsistent changes from being committed by later steps.

options.text: In a finalizing step that always runs, uploading logs and posting the outcome to the pull request
options.why: Yes. A step that runs regardless of outcome guarantees evidence exists even for failed runs - which is exactly when you need it most.

options.text: In the agent's system prompt, instructing it to report any errors it notices
options.why: No. That is guidance, not handling. An error the agent does not notice is not reported, and a prompt cannot stop a workflow.

takeaway: Handle errors at every boundary: the tool call, the workflow step and job, and a finalizer that always emits evidence.

text: Which recovery strategy does the module specifically warn against retrying, and what should happen instead?

options.text: Transient network failures - escalate immediately rather than retrying.
options.why: Backwards. Transient failures are exactly what bounded retries are for.

options.text: Security failures - investigate them rather than repeatedly retrying.
options.why: The recovery guidance lists this explicitly: retry transient failures within bounds, escalate after repeated failures, roll back quickly using small PRs and safe revert paths, and investigate security failures instead of repeatedly retrying. A blocked security check is telling you something, and retrying only hides it.

options.text: Merge conflicts - always retry until the rebase succeeds.
options.why: Repeated conflicts are an escalation trigger, not something to retry indefinitely.

options.text: Test failures - roll back the entire branch on the first failure.
options.why: A failing test is normal iteration; the agent may revise the branch within retry limits.

takeaway: Retry transient faults, escalate on repetition, roll back with small PRs - but investigate security failures rather than retrying them.

text: An escalation fires and a human is paged. What should the escalation itself contain to be useful?

options.text: A link to the failing workflow run and nothing else, to keep the notification short.
options.why: A bare link makes the human reconstruct the entire situation from scratch, which is the slow path.

options.text: What failed, what was attempted, what evidence exists, and what the suggested next step is.
options.why: This is the escalation payload the safe-iteration policy prescribes. It converts a notification into an actionable handoff and is what stops escalations becoming noise.

options.text: A full dump of the agent's reasoning trace.
options.why: A raw trace is unsummarized. The receiving human needs a decision-ready brief, with the trace available if they want it.

options.text: A request for the human to re-run the workflow and see what happens.
options.why: That delegates the diagnosis back to the human without any of the context the system already has.

takeaway: Escalate with a brief: what failed, what was tried, what evidence exists, and the suggested next step.

text: A handoff between two agents is recorded as "passed to the security agent". Why is that insufficient?

options.text: It should name the model version used by the receiving agent.
options.why: Model provenance is useful telemetry but is not what makes a handoff reviewable.

options.text: It records the transition but not the decision, the rationale, or the next owner - so a reviewer cannot tell why the handoff happened or who is accountable now.
options.why: The recommended structure captures decision, rationale, and next owner. Without those three, the handoff is an event rather than a documented decision, and accountability is ambiguous.

options.text: Handoffs should never be documented in pull requests.
options.why: The pull request is exactly where handoffs should be documented, in a standard structure.

options.text: It should be recorded in the audit log rather than the pull request.
options.why: The audit log records platform events. Design decisions and handoff rationale belong where reviewers read them.

takeaway: Document handoffs as decision, rationale, and next owner - not just as "who has it now".

text: An agent is being retired. Which steps preserve auditability and workflow continuity? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Leave the agent's configuration in git history rather than scrubbing it
options.why: Yes. Git history is the durable record of what the agent was configured to do at any point in the past.

options.text: Retain its past workflow runs and artifacts under the retention policy
options.why: Yes. Those are the evidence for anything the agent did, and deleted artifacts cannot be restored.

options.text: Document the retirement decision and reassign ownership of anything it used to handle
options.why: Yes. Lifecycle management requires clearly defined ownership, so retirement must say who now owns the work and why the agent was retired.

options.text: Delete the agent's branches and close its open pull requests without comment
options.why: No. Silent deletion destroys context. Open work should be reassigned or closed with a recorded reason so the trail stays intact.

takeaway: Retire by preserving: config in git history, runs and artifacts under retention, a documented decision, and reassigned ownership.
